knownFor: Roman emperor who, with Licinius, gave Christians freedom of worship, and who called the bishops to the council at Nicaea.

traces: Nicaea did not end the quarrel. Five bishops would not sign the creed because of the word homoousios, Eusebius of Nicomedia among them. Eusebius of Caesarea signed, he told his church, with peace in view.
Constantine also wrote to Eusebius of Caesarea asking for fifty copies of the sacred scriptures, on parchment, for the churches of the city that bore his name.
After the council he wrote to the churches that Easter must fall on one day everywhere, so that some would not be fasting while others feasted.
remembered: Eusebius honors him as the first sovereign baptized in a church of the martyrs.
The church historian Sozomen calls him a powerful protector of the Christian religion and the first emperor zealous for the church.
His letter about Easter speaks of the Jews with contempt, and Eusebius copies it whole.

uncertain: The two early tellings of the sign do not agree: Eusebius has a cross of light in the sky and then a dream, Lactantius a dream alone. Eusebius adds that at dawn Constantine called in workers in gold and precious stones to make the sign as a standard, and that he saw it with his own eyes.

Not everyone accepted Eusebius's account of the baptism. A Syriac chronicle that goes under Zachariah's name says Eusebius got it wrong. The emperor was not baptized at the end of his life, it says, since the story of his conversion by Rome's bishop, Silvester, is kept there in writing and in pictures. Pagans told yet another story, that he turned Christian to be cleansed after the killing of his son Crispus, and Sozomen calls it an invention.
